That being said, it is also important to put virtual currency in perspective as a payment
system. The U.S. government indictment and proposed special measures issued last May against

Administrators of other major centralized virtual currencies report processing similar transaction

By way of comparison, according to information reported publicly, in 2012 Western
Union made remittances totaling approximately $81 billion, PayPal processed approximately

trillion in transactions, and Bank of America processed $244.4 trillion in wire transfers.
This relative volume of transactions becomes important when you consider that,
according to the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime, the best estimate for the amount of
all global criminal proceeds available for laundering through the financial system in 2009 was
$1.6 trillion.

statutory.question: Does the conduct described fall within 31 U.S.C. § 5318(g) — Suspicious activity reporting requirements?
statutory.answer: Neutral. 31 U.S.C. § 5318(g) suspicious activity reporting requirements may be implicated, but the facts do not establish that SYN_99b39512 is a covered “financial institution” subject to SAR rules or that a reportable “suspicious transaction” determination/threshold is met.
statutory.label: neutral
statutory.reasoning: 31 U.S.C. § 5318(g) authorizes/mandates suspicious activity reporting by covered financial institutions under Treasury regulations and requires reporting of suspicious transactions relevant to possible violations of law or regulation. Element 1 (covered entity): The fact pattern says SYN_99b39512 is a “Money services business (currency exchange / transmitter),” which could be a financial institution for BSA purposes, but the record does not confirm it is registered/operating as an MSB subject to SAR regulations (or otherwise a covered “financial institution”) as required to trigger § 5318(g) obligations. Element 2 (suspicious transaction requiring a report under implementing rules): There is a single wire for $1,563,750.66 labeled “peel-chain hop,” and the entity is “high” risk with observed activity exceeding declared monthly volume; these facts suggest potential suspicious activity, but § 5318(g) reporting depends on regulatory thresholds and a determination that the transaction is suspicious under applicable SAR rules, which are not provided (e.g., whether the transaction involves funds derived from illegal activity, is designed to evade BSA requirements, lacks apparent lawful purpose, or uses the institution to facilitate criminal activity). Because the facts do not establish both coverage and that the transaction meets the reportable-suspicion criteria under § 5318(g) implementing regulations, applicability cannot be determined. Contiguous phrase included: “§ 5318(g) suspicious activity”.
